description: The Elizabethan playhouse, Shakespeare's sources and the original audiences who watched it.
content_html:
Context as a Staging Resource

When you study context in Drama, you are not studying history for its own sake. You are asking: how does knowing when and where this play was first performed change the choices a director, designer and performer might make? The Elizabethan playhouse was radically different from a modern theatre building, and those differences shaped every convention Shakespeare embedded in the text. Understanding those conventions unlocks staging choices that would otherwise seem puzzling.

Shakespeare and His Source Material

Romeo and Juliet was written around 1594–1596. Shakespeare did not invent the story: he adapted it from The Tragicall Historye of Romeus and Juliet, a narrative poem published by Arthur Brooke in 1562. Brooke’s poem was itself derived from earlier Italian novellas. What Shakespeare added was the compression of the timeline (Brooke’s poem unfolds over months; Shakespeare’s play takes five days), the elevation of Juliet’s character from passive victim to active agent, and the density of verse that makes the lovers’ language feel qualitatively different from everything around them.

For a modern director, the source material is context for a staging choice: knowing that Shakespeare deliberately accelerated the action opens up the question of how to communicate urgency visually. A minimal set with no heavy furniture changes — actors carrying small props, moving quickly through empty space — might communicate the compressed timeline more effectively than elaborate scene changes.

Key Fact

Shakespeare adapted Romeo and Juliet from Arthur Brooke’s 1562 poem. His two key changes: he compressed the action from months into five days, and he gave Juliet active agency rather than keeping her a passive figure. Both changes have direct implications for how the play is staged.

The Elizabethan Playhouse: Shared Light, Open Stage

The plays Shakespeare wrote for the Theatre, the Curtain and later the Globe (opened 1599) were performed in the afternoon, in daylight, with no stage lighting as we understand it today. This is a fundamental difference from modern theatre. The audience could see each other as clearly as they could see the performers. There was no fourth wall: the thrust stage of the Elizabethan playhouse pushed the actors into the crowd, surrounded on three sides, and direct address was the norm rather than the exception.

For a modern production that wants to recover this quality — the shared light, the direct contact between performer and audience — a theatre-in-the-round configuration or a configuration that uses the audience as part of the world of Verona can be a deliberate contextual choice. Shakespeare’s Globe in London has used “groundling” standing audience areas since its reconstruction in 1997, and productions there demonstrate how a prologue chorus speaking directly to spectators changes the play’s opening — the audience is implicated in the tragedy before the first scene begins.

When there is no stage lighting to focus attention, the performer must use their body and voice to create and direct focus. Focus in Elizabethan staging was entirely achieved through blocking, vocal projection and the spatial relationship between bodies. Soliloquies — characters speaking their private thoughts aloud — are direct descendants of this convention: the character turns from the other performers and speaks to the audience because the audience is physically present and available. Juliet’s “gallop apace” speech and Romeo’s tomb soliloquy both work differently when we understand they were originally spoken to a shared-light crowd, not delivered into the dark of a fourth-wall theatre.

A modern designer who wants to recreate this quality might use a lighting wash that covers both stage and part of the audience, rather than a clean division between light stage and dark house. This is a deliberate contextual statement: the audience shares the world of Verona.

Boy Actors and Juliet

In Elizabethan playing companies, all female roles were played by boys — apprentice actors who had not yet broken their voices. For the original performances of Romeo and Juliet, Juliet was played by a boy actor. This has several implications for modern staging decisions. First, it means the performance style was necessarily more stylised than naturalistic: a boy in a dress and wig communicates femininity through convention rather than biological correspondence. Second, it means the verse speaking — the formal, musical language of the role — was central to the performance in a way that pure emotional identification was not. The performance tradition for Juliet’s verse asks the actor to let the language do the emotional work rather than forcing psychological realism onto the lines.

For a modern performer playing Juliet using a Stanislavskian approach of emotional memory and interior truth, this history is relevant: the text was written with a different performance tradition in mind, and some of the most celebrated modern Juliets have found ways to hold the verse’s musicality alongside psychological realism, rather than flattening the verse into conversational prose delivery.

Key Fact

In Elizabethan companies, female roles including Juliet were played by boy actors. This convention means the verse speaking and the stylised nature of the role were always central to the performance, rather than biographical or naturalistic identification. Modern performers must decide how to hold the verse’s musicality alongside psychological realism.

The Patriarchal Household: Elizabethan Context and Modern Staging

Elizabethan society operated under a strongly patriarchal household structure: fathers had legal authority over their daughters, and marriage was frequently an economic and social arrangement rather than a matter of personal choice. Juliet’s father arranging her marriage to Paris without asking her was unremarkable to an original audience. An Elizabethan father’s threat to disown a disobedient daughter was a real legal and economic threat, not a hollow outburst.

This context shapes how a modern director chooses to stage the Capulet household. A production that wants to emphasise the political dimension of Juliet’s situation might design the Capulet home as a formally ordered space — rigid furniture arrangement, cold marble or stone surfaces, clear spatial hierarchies with elevated seating for Lord Capulet — that communicates the household as an institution as much as a family. Juliet’s private bedroom, by contrast, might be the only space in the design with warmth and softness: the one place that is hers. When Capulet invades that space in Act Three, the staging configuration is itself a statement about patriarchal intrusion.

Students frequently include context as a paragraph at the end of an answer: “Also, Shakespeare wrote this in the 1590s when audiences were Elizabethan.” This does not score marks. Context earns marks only when it is connected to a specific staging, design or performance choice with a justified effect on the audience.

GOOD: “Because Elizabethan audiences would have recognised the patriarchal authority of Lord Capulet’s threat as legally real, a modern director might choose to emphasise it through staging: Capulet elevated on a raised level, Juliet on the floor, a single top-light picking out Capulet alone — to communicate to a modern audience how institutionally supported that authority was, even if they no longer experience it as such.”

BAD: “In Elizabethan times, women had no rights, which is relevant because Juliet can’t marry who she wants.”

The first answer uses context to justify a staging decision. The second uses context as a fact-dump. Only the first progresses past the developing band.
exam_tip_html: On playwright’s intentions questions that ask about context, the most common error is presenting historical information without connecting it to a staging consequence. Every piece of context you cite must earn its place by linking to a specific design or performance choice and an effect on the audience. The Elizabethan shared-light stage, the boy actor convention, the patriarchal household — none of these is a stand-alone fact; each is a prompt for a staging choice. When you write about context in extended-response questions, use the formula: “Because [context], a director might [specific staging decision] to communicate [effect on audience] because [thematic meaning].” The examiner is looking for that chain of reasoning, not the historical fact in isolation. Also note that knowing Arthur Brooke’s poem as the source is useful only when you use it to explain what Shakespeare changed and why those changes matter for staging.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Shakespeare adapted Romeo and Juliet from Arthur Brooke’s 1562 poem; his key changes — compression of time, elevation of Juliet’s agency — are direct staging resources, not just literary facts.
  • The Elizabethan thrust stage, shared light and boy actor conventions all shaped how Shakespeare wrote the play; modern productions that want to recover those qualities can do so through thrust configuration, extended lighting wash and verse-centred performance approaches.
  • Context earns marks only when it is connected to a specific staging decision with a justified audience effect — fact-dumping does not progress past the developing band.

practice_questions.text: Name the author of the 1562 narrative poem that Shakespeare used as his primary source for Romeo and Juliet.
What is meant by the term 'fourth wall' in theatre?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the fourth wall as the imaginary boundary between the stage and the audience; 1 mark for explaining what 'breaking the fourth wall' means (performers acknowledge or address the audience directly, as if removing the barrier).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a designer might use a lighting wash to communicate the Elizabethan shared-light convention to a modern audience and its effect on their experience of the play.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identifying the specific lighting choice (a wash that covers stage and part of the auditorium) (1), explaining how this connects to the Elizabethan context (shared light, no fourth wall) (1), describing the effect on the audience (they feel implicated in the world of Verona) (1), linking the choice to a specific moment of the play where direct address is enhanced (1).

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer, explain how you would design the lighting for the scene in Act Three where Lord Capulet confronts Juliet in her bedroom. Refer to specific lighting choices and their contextual justification.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the student specifies at least two distinct lighting choices for the scene, naming lantern types, directions, colours and intensities; the choices are justified with reference to Elizabethan patriarchal context (Capulet’s authority being institutionally supported) and to character (Juliet in softer, warmer light to communicate vulnerability; Capulet in harsh top-light to communicate institutional power); the contrast between lighting states is described; effect on the audience is named.

Secure: the student makes concrete lighting choices, names at least one lantern direction or colour, and links the choices to the context and character with some justification; effect on audience present.

Developing: the student suggests lighting changes but in generic terms (dark, threatening lighting; warm romantic lighting for Juliet); contextual reference present but not linked to staging consequence.

Emerging: the student describes mood without naming specific lighting elements; descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Shakespeare uses the Elizabethan convention of soliloquy to communicate his intentions about Juliet's isolation and agency. Refer to at least two moments in the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the student analyses how soliloquy in the Elizabethan shared-light context is not just a literary device but a staging one (the audience is directly addressed, implicated in Juliet’s decision-making); they name two specific soliloquy moments (the balcony scene’s extended musings; the potion soliloquy in Act Four) and explain what Shakespeare intends the audience to understand about Juliet’s isolation and agency; the analysis connects Elizabethan convention to modern staging choices; judgement sustained.

Secure: the student identifies soliloquy’s function, names two moments, explains the audience’s response to Juliet’s isolation; contextual link to Elizabethan staging may be present.

Developing: the student describes what happens in soliloquy scenes without analysing Shakespeare’s intentions; context mentioned but not connected to staging.

Emerging: the student describes the scenes without analysis; minimal awareness of Shakespeare’s intentions or the audience’s experience.

practice_questions.text: You are directing a production of Romeo and Juliet in a thrust stage configuration, drawing on the Elizabethan shared-light convention. Discuss how you would use set design, staging configuration, performer choices and sound to communicate the world of Verona and the tragedy of the feud to the audience. Refer to specific staging decisions throughout.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the student designs a coherent production in a named thrust configuration, making specific choices about set design (e.g. minimal furniture representing both Montague and Capulet spaces through symbolic props rather than elaborate builds), staging configuration (the thrust bringing the audience into Verona’s streets), performer choices (direct address to the audience for soliloquies, using the audience proximity established by the thrust), and sound (a diegetic city soundscape that surrounds the audience, building the world of Verona beyond the stage edges); every choice is justified with reference to Elizabethan context and audience effect; a directorial throughline is evident; contextual knowledge is applied rather than listed.

Secure: the student makes concrete choices across most disciplines, links them to context and audience effect; some disciplines may lack full development.

Developing: the student mentions thrust staging and some design ideas but does not fully justify choices with contextual reasoning; context described rather than applied.

Emerging: the student lists staging ideas without contextual connection; descriptive rather than analytical.

knowledge_checks.q: Who wrote the 1562 narrative poem that Shakespeare used as his primary source for Romeo and Juliet?
In Elizabethan playing companies, who played the female roles including Juliet?
The imaginary boundary between the performance space and the audience is called the _____.
The Globe Theatre was opened in _____, and its stage was a thrust configuration surrounded on three sides by the audience.
Match each piece of context to its staging consequence.
right: Verse-centred performance style rather than purely naturalistic emotional identification
Lighting wash extended into the auditorium, dissolving the fourth wall
Capulet on a raised level, Juliet on the floor, to externalise institutionally supported authority

flashcard_questions.q: Who wrote the 1562 poem Shakespeare adapted for Romeo and Juliet?
Approximately when did Shakespeare write Romeo and Juliet?
What are the two key changes Shakespeare made to Brooke's source poem?
flashcard_questions.a: He compressed months into five days and gave Juliet active agency.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Elizabethan convention for casting female roles?
flashcard_questions.a: Boy apprentice actors played all female roles.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the fourth wall in theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: The imaginary boundary between performers and the audience.

flashcard_questions.q: What staging configuration did the Elizabethan Globe use?
flashcard_questions.a: A thrust stage, with the audience surrounding three sides of the stage.
A stage that protrudes into the audience, surrounded on three sides.
A configuration where the audience surrounds the performance area on all sides.
The direction of an audience's attention, achieved through lighting, blocking or performance.
A broad, even spread of light covering a large area of the stage.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a Stanislavskian approach to performance?
flashcard_questions.a: A system for achieving psychological truthfulness using emotional memory and inner life.
The physical relationship between the performing area and the audience — e.g. thrust, in-the-round, proscenium.

glossary_terms.definition: The imaginary boundary between the performance space and the audience; breaking it means performers acknowledge or address the audience directly.
A staging configuration in which the stage protrudes into the audience, which sits on three sides of the performance area.
A staging arrangement in which the audience surrounds the performing area on all sides, eliminating a single front-facing viewpoint.
The direction in which an audience's attention is drawn at any given moment, achieved through lighting, blocking, sound or performance.
The planned physical placement and movement of performers on stage, determined by the director to control focus and meaning.
A broad, even spread of light covering a large area of the stage, often used to include the auditorium in a shared-light effect.
Relating to the system developed by Constantin Stanislavski for achieving psychological truthfulness in performance through emotional memory and inner life.
The physical relationship between the performing area and the audience, shaped by the theatre space and the director's choices.
